title: Catching the ox
hook: picture four: caught, but it pulls hard (Ox-Herding 4)
tomorrow: what did one Zen teacher tell a brand-new monk to do?

segments.voice: Yesterday, a glimpse: a bird on a branch, a pebble on bamboo, the ox seen at last. Seen isn't the same as held.

Quit a habit, and the second week can be the loud one. The thing you walked away from starts calling louder than before. That's the answer to yesterday's question, and it's Kuoan's fourth picture. The herder has finally got a rope around the ox. He's holding it with everything he has. And the ox is pulling the other way. Not because he failed to see it. Because he did.
screen: `THE SECOND WEEK.` → `A ROPE AROUND THE OX.` → `IT PULLS THE OTHER WAY.`

segments.voice: The preface says it plainly. Long hidden in the wild, today the ox is met. But the world around still draws it; it keeps longing for the sweet-smelling grass. Stubborn, wild, hard to keep. And notice what the ox wants: nothing wicked, just the sweet grass, the old familiar field. To bring it round, he has to use the whip. In the verse he holds on with all his strength, and still the ox sometimes charges up onto the high plateau, sometimes vanishes into the misty mountains. Buddhist teachers have a name for that pull: vasana, habit energy, the leftover push of old actions in the mind. Some readers compare it to a scent that stays in a cloth after the flowers are gone. Here's the teaching, in Zen's own order. Seeing your nature doesn't erase old habits. That's why the pulling comes after the glimpse, not before it. And notice what Kuoan doesn't say. He never says the herder failed, or that the glimpse was false. Catching is the stage of pulling. On this map, a hard stretch after a breakthrough doesn't mean the ox is gone. It means the rope is finally in your hands, and the ox has noticed.
screen: `STILL LONGING FOR SWEET GRASS.` · `UP THE PLATEAU, INTO THE MIST.` · `VASANA: HABIT ENERGY.` · `PULLING COMES AFTER SEEING.` · then, large: `IT PULLS.`

segments.voice: Hold your hands in front of you as if they grip a rope, and feel the tug each time your attention pulls toward a sound, a plan, an itch. Don't yank back; just keep the grip, steady and close. If your hardest year comes to mind, let it be one more tug on the rope.
Catching the ox: Kuoan's fourth picture. The rope is on, and the ox still pulls toward the sweet grass.
Pocket this one: it pulls, and the pulling comes after the seeing, not instead of it. See you at picture five.

howItsDone: Zen and other Buddhist teachers speak of habit energy that stays after insight, and keep training after a first awakening. People on this path expect the pull and keep hold of their practice through it.
